new_statements.quote: T one was shown to be phonemic in E. Kewa (Kewa I:27). Tonal patterns in W. Kewa correspond to those in E. Kewa with the exception that a low-low pattern occurs on verb stems and must be reconstructed only in the case of nouns. [...] The perceptual or auditory height of a tone may be conditioned by stress placement (cf. Kewa I:28). Disregarding levels above the phonemic word, a primary stress occurs on the first syllable of any noun stem of less than four syllables and on the second syllable of any stem over four. Any basic low tone which occurs on such stressed syllables will be heard as mid. [p.28-29, Kewa I:] Stress is non-phonemic. The most pronounced stress occurs on the first syllable of words, except verbs where it may occur elsewhere.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kewa is a two-tone (high/low) language with extensive tone sandhi; stress is non-contrastive and falls on the first syllable of nouns (and pronouns, adjectives, time words) of up to three syllables, on the second syllable of longer stems; verb stress position depends on tone class and affixation; each phonological foot carries one obligatory stress, phrase stress on the first foot.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Kewa I (p.29 of dictionary): high tone, fortis consonants and /aa/ 'produce a minor stress if they occur on unstressed syllables'; no positional secondary-stress rule (Yarapea 2006 gives penult secondary stress for East Kewa words over five syllables).
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs: stress by tone class (Class I final/second syllable, Class II penult, Class III second stem syllable, Class IV antepenult; negative prefix na- attracts stress in some classes), pp.38-39; clitic -re 'always stressed'; adjacent stresses within a phrase are suppressed (Kewa II p.32).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is for the phonemic word 'disregarding levels above'; foot/phrase levels treated separately (Kewa II). CRITICAL IDENTITY CAVEAT: the evidential base is West Kewa (1971 grammar, Usa) and East Kewa (Kewa I/II, Muli); the dictionary treats South Kewa (Erave/Pole) as a dialect of the same language and includes its lexicon, but gives no prosodic data from the South dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: erav1244 Erave = South Kewa = 'Pole' (Franklin 1971:7 n.3 'Pole is the southernmost dialect of Kewa'; APCM/UFM mission at Erave). All accessible prosodic statements (Franklin & Franklin 1962 'Kewa I', J. Franklin 1965 'Kewa II' = East Kewa east2516, Muli; Franklin 1971 grammar = West Kewa west2599, Usa; Yarapea 2006 = East Kewa) describe the sister dialects that Glottolog splits off as separate languages. The 1978 dictionary nominally covers the South dialect too but its phonology section contains no South Kewa data. Entering the quoted rule under erav1244 would re-count the same W/E Kewa statement already attributable to west2599/east2516.

sources.note: Explicitly East dialect only (p.1). Sec. 2.2.1 pp.28-29: stress predictable, non-phonemic; 1st syllable stressed in 1-3-syllable words, 2nd in 4-syllable words, 3rd in longer words; secondary stress on penult of words over five syllables. Not applicable to Erave except by analogy.
